text.p: Wilson Kipketer used to paint to pay for his school tuition.

On Friday the slight Kenyan, who will become a Danish citizen in December, produced a masterpiece when he shattered the 800 metres indoor world record during a preliminary heat at the world championships.
And like any great work of art, this one will reward Kipketer for his effort to the tune of $50,000 for breaking the world mark.
The 26-year-old athlete is almost certain to add to his bank account with another $50,000 as the winner of Sunday's final.
Despite growing up in Kenya in near poverty, money has never been the motivating factor in Kipketer's athletics career.

In 1995 when Denmark's top athletes were invited to dinner by the mayor of Copenhagen, Kipketer arrived at the reception riding his bicycle, despite having just won a new car for his 800 metres victory at the outdoor world championships earlier that year.

"It didn't matter about the money, I was going to race here anyway," said Kipketer, after rocketing around the Bercy track in one minute, 43.96 seconds to better the old mark of 1:44.84 set by Kenyan Paul Ereng in 1989.
"Even if there was no money there was still a championship. This is my job, every year I have to get better."
Kipketer once painted a school in order to pay for his tuition.
Discovered by Kip Keino, the great Kenyan middle distance runner put the promising Kipketer in touch with Father Colm, headmaster of St Patrick's Boy's School in Item, Ireland.
Father Colm eventually agreed to pay Kipketer's tuition on the condition that he painted the school during holidays.
A victory in Sunday's final will set up a showdown at this summer's outdoor championships with Scandinavian rival and Olympic champion Vebjorn Rodal of Norway.
"I didn't miss him being here, I don't miss anyone," said Kipketer. "I sometimes miss what is inside me. I have my own rules."
One rule appears to be keeping secrets.
Kipketer trained secretly in the United States before arriving in Paris on Monday and refusing to reveal the location.
"It's my secret and if I tell you it won't be anymore," said Kipketer. "It's something I keep close."
